This article hit home for me. I grew up in New England during a time ticks were confined to certain areas. My fantasy was to live forever in the woods and fields. That is over.

He was referred to a litany of specialists by his PMD in quick succession (hematologist for his low platelets, cardiologist and neurologist after he felt faint one day. When the body rash started to appear, we were told to try and get in to see a dermatologist.). With a stroke of a pen, my unwell father was condemned to dayslong sidequest to get a diagnosis. When things really got bad the emergency department included Lyme testing in their work up. But it was not until he was coughing up blood in the ICU, with a platelet count of 4,000, that someone thought to test for OTHER tickborne diseases. He was PCR positive for anaplasmosis. The torture started to finally end within hours of his first dose of doxycycline. After he recovered (in a much physically diminished state)…multiple people in town shared that they had had anaplasmosis…..including his PMD! If the PMD had just ordered a tickborne disease PANEL early, it would have prevented so much suffering. I am still fuming.

Hospitals spent nearly twice as much on administration ($687 billion) as they did on direct patient care ($346 billion) in 2023.  Administrative costs rose from 65% to 66.5% of total hospital expenditures over that same period.

It is time for hospitals to take a haircut and get their house in order by trimming the fat just like every other segment of the health care industry has had to do.

It was killed by a stallion the following day, and the coyotes ate the carcass. As sad as that was, we realized that these are feral animals. It’s also important to know that horses are unlike pets. They’re large. They’re expensive. It takes skill and strength to safely handle and train them. You can’t just put one in your yard and pop on a saddle, and they’re hard to rehome. So when overpopulation becomes a problem, it’s not easy to solve. I didn’t mind buying a manure fork, but many people do. All those mustangs were removed, and that was 20 years ago. The dart guns for population control are a great advance, but like everything else, that involves money, time, and skill. While intended to bypass obstruction, political scientists warned it would permanently alter the lifetime appointment process. When Republicans later extended this logic to Supreme Court appointments, the 60-vote bipartisan threshold was completely dismantled, transforming confirmation battles into hyper-partisan fights.

This environment produces judges under immense ideological pressure to satisfy political bases. For example, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson's rulings and dissents frequently lean into progressive policy positions, reinforcing public perceptions of a politicized bench. Been on 15+ antidepressants over the years and many augmentative ones like the antipsychotics. Because I have restless leg syndrome, many atypical antidepressants and antipsychotics trigger my legs due to their effects on the dopamine receptors. 

I've tried TMS. It helped while I was going through treatment but insurance does not cover maintenance treatments, so the effects wore off after a month. The only drug that has ever helped me is Auvelity (dextromorphan/Wellbutrin). It worked very fast, and while I'm not in remission I felt I was there for the first few weeks. It still helps a lot, more than any other. It's an NMDA antagonist like psysilobim, probably why it has helped me. I plan to try more NMDA antagonist as they come out in the years to come.

For what it's worth to others, learn your brain chemistry. See what the drugs you are taking are supposed to do and how you react, and what the neurotransmitters in your brain do. I determined I have dopamine deficiencies due to anhedonia still being a thing, so I am going to try a dopamine agonist at small doses to just see. Do your research, look at journals and studies, and advocate for yourself.

I'd love to try Ketamine, but being the sole driver and not having any family or friends who could help me drive it is not possible.

It is unfortunate that this article does not mention the full range of options for treatment resistant depression. 

Although TMS, ketamine/esketamine, and psychedelics (e.g. psilocybin) have received much recent publicity, ECT remains the gold standard of care for severe treatment resistant depression or catatonia. Many patients benefit from a tricyclic antidepressant (e.g., nortriptyline or imipramine)  or a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) (e.g., phenelzine, tranylcypromine) but have never been offered one of these. Every individual with treatment resistant depression should also receive treatment with an evidence based treatment such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Psychotherapy is not just chatting about day-to-day aspects of one's week but should  be a structured and evidence based approach to gaining insight into (and modifying) one's thought processes and behavior. These can be especially engrained with treatment resistant depression and can take years of concerted effort to establish new patterns of coping/interaction.  

Two messages deserve emphasis: 
1. For individuals with treatment resistant depression, there are many more options than discussed in this article! Don't lose hope!!!
2. For anyone involved in health policy and payment (such as insurers), please authorize appropriate treatments for treatment resistant depression. Although months/years of psychotherapy or meds/ECT/TMS may be required, the benefits for patients and society can be huge!

I think there are two reasons. First, both Democrats and Republicans have become mercantilist, favoring tariff walls to shield industries in their congressional districts and states. This is too bad—it will result in mediocre and overpriced products compared to what they would be with better competition—but how many lawmakers know much about economics? Probably few.

The other reason is that the tariffs are a national sales tax, similar to the value-added taxes that Canada and Europe have. A national sales that called itself that would be politically untenable and couldn’t get through Congress. But a back-door sales tax in the form of tariffs gets over political hurdles.

With a $40 trillion debt, the U.S. is desperate for any revenue it can find, and our tariff-based national sales tax is bringing in money. “The U.S. government collected roughly $195 billion in customs duties and tariffs during fiscal year 2025, a sharp increase over prior years.” (AI overview.) comments.body:
So, just exactly what are the concerns these folks have? 

"Feelings" and personal "fears" are not substantive reasons to not build data process and storage facilities that are already integral to everyone's use of our publicly provided, national Internet infrastructure.  Frankly, hand wavy, generalized "concerns" don't cut it.  Noise, for instance, can be readily cuantified; a 40 db limit at property line is decidedly not intrusive, power demand that is generated on-site not only doesn't impact local energy generative capacity, it actually adds capacity to the local supply system at zero cost to the local economy. 

There is a raft of unwarranted, knee-jerk, reaction floating around on the impact of large scale data storage and processing installations; your journalistic attention would be better served by reporting on the facts of the matter rather than on the whimsical fantasies of poorly informed Junior High School kids.

My advice to Brazilians is to pick one: global power or shared prosperity. Don't prioritize both. They don't go together.

To be a global power means giving control to corporations that can create economic power. All other power comes from that. That's how the US became the most powerful nation in the history of the world.

Does the US have shared prosperity? Hah! Those same corporations will hog the prosperity for themselves.

It's better to be like Singapore. Wealthy, everyone gets a share, not particularly potent on the world stage. If you have enough money, you can arrange for others to value your security (and the money they have invested) enough that another country won't invade and steal all your stuff. Banks are like every other corporation. I’m upset with the financial institution where our retirement funds are vulnerable to thieves. Don’t get me started on the offers I’ve received offering credit monitoring for a period of time. But many banks give short shrift to data security, for one or more of the following reasons:  1) Ignorance  -  few bank execs are grounded in IT security, thus overlook the risks.  2) Data security does not generate revenue.  A robust data security system costs money to set up and maintain.  3) Banks don't want to "inconvenience" their customers with pesky multi-factor authentication, for fear of losing them to a competitor.

The broker's description of the Stamford house includes the following "While the field card lists the property as 2 bedrooms and 2.5 bathrooms, the home currently offers 4 bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms, providing substantially more space and functionality than the public record reflects."  This language makes me wonder, why not just correct the "field card" (in broker speak) or the public records? It makes me think that other possible ways to describe the situation would be to say, the house contains 2 illegal bedrooms and 1 illegal bathroom (or 2 half-baths), or to say 2 bedrooms and 1 bathroom are not covered by the C of 0. The broker's language is much more elegant. I note that the NY Times description just goes with the 4 bedroom, 3.5 bathroom description. I hope that potential buyers look into this situation. articles.title: ‘A Guide to Open Water Lifesaving’ Review: The Rescuer Needed Rescue
articles.summary: The author scoured the literature on PTSD in a quest to help her partner. She found that becoming a caregiver held its own perils.

comments.name: Mitchell K
comments.body: The impact of any type of long term care requirements on a non paid caregiver of this sort are very real.  It is not just carrying for someone with PTSD.  Caring for someone who has addiction problems, or dementia, or a physical malady is a very draining task filled with exhaustion and difficult emotions to process.  Most people who have been through it do not have a “team” to discuss options with, they just do what they think is necessary and figure they will get through it.  Very little in our existing medical system, and almost nothing in medical insurance, helps in these situation when it comes to day to day living.
